name: Provisions of Oxford, Baronial Reform
summary: English barons under Simon de Montfort force Henry III to accept the Provisions of Oxford, a constitutional settlement more radical than Magna Carta. The provisions establish a permanent council of 15 barons with regular meetings, requiring the king to govern with their consent. Parliament is to meet three times a year. The provisions are suspended and re-imposed multiple times; the Second Barons' War (1264-1267) follows, with de Montfort's parliament (1265) representing the first parliament including knights and burgesses.

_quarry.structural_significance: The Provisions of Oxford and de Montfort's parliament establish the parliamentary precedent that becomes the model for English constitutional development; the concept of representation, knights of the shire and burgesses alongside magnates, is institutionalized even before Edward I's Model Parliament (1295); the reforms demonstrate that English baronage could unite against royal overreaching in ways French or German nobles could not
